passage: When Amandeep's grandfather died, the whole village came to the house. Ojas, his friend from the next lane, stood near the gate, unsure whether to go in. He'd known Bauji since he was small; the old man used to give them sugarcane from his field. Inside, Amandeep sat very still, eyes dry, while women sang and neighbours brought food. Ojas sat beside him and said nothing. After the cremation, Amandeep finally spoke. "I didn't even cry. Is something wrong with me?" Ojas shook his head. A week later they walked to the sugarcane field, and Amandeep cut a stalk and suddenly sat down in the mud and cried for a long time. Ojas stayed until he stood up.

qa.q: What did Bauji use to give the boys?
qa.a: He used to give them sugarcane from his field.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep ask if something was wrong with him?
qa.a: He felt confused and maybe guilty that he hadn't cried at the funeral, as if his grief didn't look the way it should.

qa.q: What did Ojas get right in supporting Amandeep?
qa.a: He stayed close, didn't force him to talk or cry, and was there when the grief finally came out in the field.

qa.q: Why might the field bring out Amandeep's tears when the funeral didn't?
qa.a: The field was full of personal memories of Bauji, while the crowded funeral may have felt too formal or overwhelming to grieve freely.

grounding: It shows a teen facing his first loss, grieving in his own time, supported by a friend.

passage: Camila's dog, Pepa, died on a rainy Tuesday in Lima. She was fourteen and had had Pepa since she was four. At school she said nothing. She didn't want to be the girl crying about a dog. Her friend Gabriel noticed she didn't eat lunch. "Is it Pepa?" he asked quietly. He had walked the dog with her twice. Camila's throat closed. She nodded. "Everyone says it's just a pet." Gabriel shrugged. "She was yours for ten years. That's not just." That weekend Camila made a small album of Pepa's photos. Gabriel came over and they looked at it together, laughing at one with Pepa wearing a paper hat. Camila cried and laughed at the same time. It felt strange but okay.

qa.q: How long had Camila had Pepa?
qa.a: She had Pepa since she was four, about ten years.

qa.q: Why did Camila say nothing at school at first?
qa.a: She feared people would think her grief over a dog was silly and didn't want to be seen crying about it.

qa.q: How did Gabriel's words help Camila?
qa.a: By saying ten years together was not "just" a pet, he validated her sadness and made it easier for her to open up.

qa.q: How might Gabriel feel looking at the album with Camila?
qa.a: He probably felt sad too, since he had walked Pepa, but also glad to be trusted with Camila's memories. 🤍

grounding: It shows a teen grieving her first pet and finding a way to mourn with a friend's support.

passage: In Class 10, Gopika's classmate died in a road accident during the summer holidays. When school reopened, his desk stood empty near the window. Nobody sat there. The teachers said a few words at assembly, then lessons went on. Gopika felt strange, angry that everything was normal. Her friend Manjula found her in the library one lunch break, not reading. "I keep looking at his desk," Gopika said. The school counsellor had put up a notice about a remembrance corner. Manjula said, "Let's write something there." They each wrote a note: Gopika about how he always lent her pencils, Manjula about his terrible jokes. Other students added notes over the week. Gopika still looked at the desk, but it felt a little less empty.

qa.q: What did Gopika write in her note about her classmate?
qa.a: She wrote about how he always lent her pencils.

qa.q: Why did Gopika feel angry when lessons went on?
qa.a: It felt wrong to her that life at school seemed normal when her classmate was gone, as if his absence wasn't being honoured.

qa.q: How did the remembrance corner help the students grieve?
qa.a: It gave them a shared, safe place to put their memories into words, so the loss was recognised together.

qa.q: How might Manjula be feeling in this situation?
qa.a: Manjula is probably grieving too, and suggesting the notes was a way to support Gopika and share that grief at once.

grounding: It shows teens facing the loss of a classmate and finding a shared way to mourn at school.

passage:
Dear Yusuf,
You asked how I'm doing since Ammamma died. Honestly, I don't know. It's been three weeks. Some days I'm fine and then I hear a pressure cooker whistle and I cry because she always shouted 'Reena, turn it off!' Isn't that silly?
Amma gave me her green shawl. I sleep with it. It still smells of her coconut oil.
On Sunday, I tried making her tomato rasam from memory. It was too sour, and Appa laughed, and then he cried too. We sat in the kitchen together for a long time. That helped more than anything.
I've started writing down her sayings in a notebook so I don't forget.
Write back soon. Tell me about your new school.
Reena

qa.q: What did Amma give Reena that belonged to Ammamma?
qa.a: Her green shawl, which still smells of her coconut oil.

qa.q: Why did Reena cry when she heard a pressure cooker whistle?
qa.a: It reminded Reena of Ammamma shouting 'Reena, turn it off!', bringing the loss back suddenly.

qa.q: Which of Reena's ways of mourning could help other grieving teens?
qa.a: Keeping a meaningful object, cooking a family recipe and writing down the person's sayings.

qa.q: How might Appa have felt in the kitchen after laughing at the rasam?
qa.a: He was grieving Ammamma too, and sharing the moment with Reena let his own tears come.

grounding: A teen writes about grieving a grandmother and the ways the family mourns.

passage: You know how everyone says 'it was just a cat'? Mitthu wasn't just a cat to me. I'm Preeti, I'm sixteen, and I had him since I was seven. Last month he got sick and the vet said he was very old. My brother Vijay and I sat with him on the balcony till the end. After that, I didn't want to talk to anyone. At school a girl said, 'Get a new one,' and I wanted to scream. What helped? Vijay and I buried him under the neem tree and planted marigolds. I made a small photo album. And I let myself cry in the shower without feeling stupid. It's still sore, but lighter. I talk to him sometimes. Is that weird?

qa.q: Where did Preeti and Vijay bury Mitthu?
qa.a: Under the neem tree, where they planted marigolds.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel when a girl told her to 'get a new one'?
qa.a: Preeti was angry and hurt, because the comment dismissed how much Mitthu meant.

qa.q: What helped Preeti mourn in a healthy way?
qa.a: Burying him with a small ritual, making a photo album and allowing tears without shame.

qa.q: If you were the girl who said 'Get a new one', what would a kinder response have been?
qa.a: Saying 'I'm sorry, you had him for so long' would acknowledge that Preeti's grief was real.

grounding: A teen tells how they grieved a pet and found ways to mourn.
